arml-2004-individual-01.title: Add the equations
arml-2004-individual-01.body:
Rewrite the system as $a-b=2$, $b-c=3$, $c-d=4$, $d-e=5$. Adding gives $a-e=14$, so $a=e+14$ and $a+e=2e+14$. Since $a=e+14\le10$ we need $e\le-4$, and $e\ge-10$. The least value is at $e=-10$: $a=4$, $b=2$, $c=-1$, $d=-5$, all in the set and distinct, so $a+e=-6$.

**Answer: -6**

arml-2004-individual-01.title: Express in terms of $d$
arml-2004-individual-01.body:
From the equations $a=b+2$, $c=b-3$, $d=c-4=b-7$, $e=d-5=b-12$, so $a+e=2b-10$ and $b=d+7$, $a+e=2d+4$. To minimise, take $d$ as small as possible with all numbers in range: $e=d-5\ge-10$ gives $d\ge-5$, so $a+e=2(-5)+4=-6$ (with $b=2$, $a=4$, $c=-1$, $e=-10$ all valid and distinct).

**Answer: -6**

arml-2004-individual-02.title: Equilateral triangle of chords
arml-2004-individual-02.body:
The three chords are equidistant from $O$ and spaced by $120^\circ$, so the lines containing them form an equilateral triangle $MNP$ with center $O$. The small circle at $O$ is its incircle; let its radius be $r$. The circumradius of this triangle is $ON=2r$.

Each outer small circle (radius $r$) is tangent to two of the lines at a vertex, say $N$, where the angle of the triangle is $60^\circ$; its center $R$ lies on the extension of $ON$ beyond $N$ with $NR=\dfrac{r}{\sin30^\circ}=2r$, so $OR=4r$. This circle is tangent internally to the unit circle, so $1=OR+r=5r$ and $r=\dfrac15$.

The area of a small circle is $\pi r^2=\dfrac{\pi}{25}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi}{25}$**

arml-2004-individual-03.title: Rhombus with equal diagonals
arml-2004-individual-03.body:
Subtracting the two equations gives $(x-k)^2-x^2=0$, so $x=\dfrac k2$. Substituting into the second ellipse: $\dfrac{k^2}{36}+y^2=1$, so $y=\dfrac{\sqrt{36-k^2}}{6}$ for $A$ (and $-y$ for $C$), hence $AC=\dfrac{\sqrt{36-k^2}}3$.

$B=(k-3,0)$ is the left intercept of the first ellipse and $D=(3,0)$ is the right intercept of the second, so $BD=6-k$. Since $AC$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BD$ (by symmetry) $ABCD$ is a rhombus, and it is a square exactly when $BD=AC$:
$$6-k=\frac{\sqrt{36-k^2}}{3}\ \Rightarrow\ 9(6-k)^2=(6-k)(6+k)\ \Rightarrow\ 54-9k=6+k\ \text{ (for }k\ne6)\Rightarrow\ k=\frac{24}5.$$
($k=6$ is rejected: the ellipses would only touch.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{24}{5}$**

arml-2004-individual-04.title: Take the reciprocal of the fractional part
arml-2004-individual-04.body:
Since $1<\sqrt[3]2<2$, $a=1$. Then $\sqrt[3]2-1=\dfrac1{b+\cdots}$ so $b<\dfrac1{\sqrt[3]2-1}<b+1$, i.e. $b=\left\lfloor\dfrac1{\sqrt[3]2-1}\right\rfloor$. Rationalising with $x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1)$ for $x=\sqrt[3]2$:
$$\frac1{\sqrt[3]2-1}=\frac{\sqrt[3]4+\sqrt[3]2+1}{2-1}=\sqrt[3]4+\sqrt[3]2+1.$$
Now $1.25^3=1.953<2<1.26^3\approx2.0004$ and $1.58^3\approx3.94<4<1.59^3\approx4.02$, so $3.83<1+\sqrt[3]2+\sqrt[3]4<3.85$, which lies between $3$ and $4$. Hence $b=3$.

**Answer: 3**

arml-2004-individual-05.title: Regular octagon minus a vertex
arml-2004-individual-05.body:
Multiplying by $x-1$: $(x-1)(x^7+\dots+1)=x^8-1$. So the solutions are the eighth roots of unity except $x=1$: the vertices of a regular octagon inscribed in the unit circle with the vertex $A=(1,0)$ removed, leaving the heptagon $BCDEFGH$.

Split the heptagon from the center $O$ into six triangles with central angle $45^\circ$, each of area $\frac12\cdot1\cdot1\cdot\sin45^\circ=\frac{\sqrt2}4$, plus the right triangle $BOH$ (central angle $90^\circ$) of area $\frac12$. Total
$$6\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{4}+\frac12=\frac{3\sqrt2+1}{2}.$$
So $a=3,b=2,c=1,d=2$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3\sqrt2+1}{2}$**

arml-2004-individual-06.title: Use the period of Fibonacci mod 4
arml-2004-individual-06.body:
Since $i^{2004}=(i^4)^{501}=1$, each term is $i^{2004-a_j}=\dfrac1{i^{a_j}}$, and $i^{a_j}$ depends only on $a_j\bmod 4$. The Fibonacci sequence mod $4$ is $1,1,2,3,1,0,1,1,\dots$, repeating every $6$ terms. One period contributes
$$\frac1i+\frac1i+\frac1{i^2}+\frac1{i^3}+\frac1{i}+\frac1{i^0}=-i-i-1+i-i+1=-2i.$$
Since $2004=6\cdot334$, the sum is $334\cdot(-2i)=-668i$.

**Answer: $-668i$**

arml-2004-individual-07.title: Interval of width 2
arml-2004-individual-07.body:
The inequality is $-\dfrac n{2004}<\dfrac{nx}{2004}-1<\dfrac n{2004}$, i.e. $\dfrac{2004}{n}-1<x<\dfrac{2004}{n}+1$, an open interval of length $2$ centered at $\dfrac{2004}n$.

If $n\mid2004$ the endpoints are integers, so the open interval contains exactly one integer (its center). If $n\nmid2004$ the endpoints are not integers, and an interval of length $2$ with non-integer endpoints contains exactly two integers. So the answer is $2004$ minus the number of divisors of $2004=2^2\cdot3\cdot167$, which is $3\cdot2\cdot2=12$: $2004-12=1992$.

**Answer: 1992**

arml-2004-individual-08.title: Cases on A's sequence
arml-2004-individual-08.body:
By symmetry (swap H and T), the cases HH and TT have the same probability of an $A$-win, and so do HT and TH. Compute each as $P(A)\cdot\sum_B P(B)\cdot P(A\text{ wins})$.

**$A=$HH** (probability $\frac14$). $B$ ends with TT w.p. $\frac14$, TH w.p. $\frac14$, HT w.p. $\frac12$ (if $B$'s first flip is H, $B$ continues until a T).
- $B=$TT: symmetric, $A$ wins with probability $\frac12$.
- $B=$TH: if a T comes first, $A$ loses (HH can only appear after a T has been followed by H, which already completes TH); if H comes first, the next flip decides, so $A$ wins with probability $\frac12\cdot\frac12=\frac14$.
- $B=$HT: flips continue until an H appears; then $A$ wins with probability $\frac12$ (next flip H).

So $A$ wins with probability $\dfrac14\left(\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac12+\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac14+\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac7{64}$. The same holds for TT.

**$A=$HT** (probability $\frac14$). $B=$HH w.p. $\frac14$; $B=$TT w.p. $\frac38$ (directly as TT w.p. $\frac14$, or as HTT w.p. $\frac18$); $B=$TH w.p. $\frac38$ (directly w.p. $\frac14$, or as HTH w.p. $\frac18$).
- $B=$HH: $C$ flips until an H appears; then the next flip decides (H gives HH, T gives HT), so $A$ wins with probability $\frac12$.
- $B=$TT: if an H is flipped first then $A$ wins; if T first, $A$'s later chance is $\frac12$, so $A$ wins with probability $\frac12+\frac14=\frac34$.
- $B=$TH: if H first $A$ wins; if T first $A$ loses, so $\frac12$.

So $A$ wins with probability $\dfrac14\left(\dfrac14\cdot\dfrac12+\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac34+\dfrac38\cdot\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac{19}{128}$; the same holds for TH.

Total: $2\left(\dfrac7{64}+\dfrac{19}{128}\right)=\dfrac{33}{64}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{33}{64}$**

arml-2004-individual-tb1.title: Similar triangles
arml-2004-individual-tb1.body:
Let $AC=b$, $BC=a$. Since $\triangle DEB\sim\triangle ACB$, $\dfrac{DE}{EB}=\dfrac{AC}{CB}$, i.e. $\dfrac{1/5}{a-1/5}=\dfrac ba$. Cross-multiplying: $\dfrac a5=b\left(a-\dfrac15\right)$, so $a+b=5ab$. The area gives $\frac12ab=\frac1{12}$, so $ab=\frac16$ and $a+b=\dfrac56$.

**Answer: $\dfrac56$**

arml-2004-individual-tb2.title: Find the domain of one piece
arml-2004-individual-tb2.body:
$\sin^{-1}$ is defined on $[-1,1]$, so we need $-1\le2\sin x\le1$, i.e. $-\frac12\le\sin x\le\frac12$. Near $x=0$ this is $x\in\left[-\frac\pi6,\frac\pi6\right]$. The endpoints of this piece are $\left(-\frac\pi6,-\frac\pi2\right)$ and $\left(\frac\pi6,\frac\pi2\right)$ (all other pieces are translates by multiples of $\pi$ or reflections, with the same endpoint distance). Their distance is
$$\sqrt{\left(\frac\pi3\right)^2+\pi^2}=\frac{\pi\sqrt{10}}{3}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{\pi\sqrt{10}}{3}$**

arml-2004-individual-tb3.title: Find the pattern
arml-2004-individual-tb3.body:
$a_1=1.0999$ has $1$ zero and $a_2=1.10000999$ has $4$ zeros. Each additional pair of blocks adds one more block $5678+5321=10999$, which extends the string of zeros by $3$ (the carry turns the preceding $9$s into $0$s while the last block ends in $999$). So $a_n$ has $1+3(n-1)$ zeros, and for $n=2004$ that is $1+3\cdot2003=6010$. (This was also confirmed by direct computation of $a_{2004}$.)

**Answer: 6010**
